newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Igloos, bulls inspire cars of tomorrow.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Igloos, bulls inspire cars of tomorrow.

text.p: There's a tram for Japan that looks like a bar, a luxury igloo for couples on the move and a sensual Superbike inspired by Spanish bulls.
A Frenchman has put the Riviera on wheels while a Greek-Scot has dreamed up a motor for the millionaire who knows what he wants and really wants to flaunt it.
From New Zealand: a Sony-mobile that looks like a stereo but sounds like a car while "a new-wave citizen" has re-designed society to fit around his politically correct London taxi, vintage 2037.
The vehicle of tomorrow might be zany, environmentally friendly, sleek or stylish -- but never dull when design students bend their imaginations.

"You might not think it's pretty but I defy anyone to say it's bland. Students can come up with crazy concepts but I wanted to create something that people could actually believe in," said Per Selvaag.

His taxi is for 2037, when he is 65 and old people are no longer "throwaways". It is for the day when "green" cars are necessary, not trendy, and when public transport will neither strain a muscle nor crick a neck.
"My taxi is extremely tall -- people keep growing -- and whether you're old or young, fit or crippled, this vehicle allows communal travel without strain," he said.
Part-Korean, part-Norwegian, Selvaag is one of a group of design students whose vision of mobility in the 21st century went on view in London last week.

While their designs might just be dreams, the Royal College of Art (RCA) -- the world's top vehicle design school -- expects its students to be snapped up by the auto industry as head hunters tour the exhibit.
SUPERBIKE INSPIRED BY A BULL
Josep Rubau's Superbike is the star of the show.

"This is a motorbike inspired by the bull, such a strong animal, so the rider becomes a bullfighter who wants to show everyone that he can control this crazy animal," said Rubau, from Figueres in Spain.

"I wanted to translate the nervous tension and stress of riding a bull into the feeling you get when this bike is beneath you. Yes, it is very, very macho but its lines are very clean and it offer many sensations," said Rubau.
Bertrand Bach's creation is also European in a market often shaped by Asia and the United States, although his car exudes more French fun than Spanish sensuality.

"It's a leisure vehicle inspired by the Riviera. This car is fun and open but in good taste. It is definitely not Californian. It has a French spirit and is designed to make people feel free and comfortable," he said.
Like the Citroen 2CV, another cheap runaround that became a design classic, luxuries are out.
There is no heater, no stereo and no doors.
"There's nothing to steal so you don't lock it. This is a really free car," said 24-year-old Bach.
CONTRASTING VISION
George Saridakis' vision is anything but.
His 200,000 pound ($326,000) car is a toy for showoffs who want the sportiness of today's Alfa Romeo rarified by the wooden elegance of the 1920s tourer.
Sumptuous maple usually seen on only the best dashboards is veneered onto the entire flank of his elegant tourer, allowing for maximum ostentation.

"It looks back at the era of motoring when it was new and exciting and the bourgeousie bought expensive cars and tailored them to their own taste," he said. "You hear so many apocalyptical views about cars these days, so I'm trying to celebrate motoring."
Saridakis doubts his car will ever be made but the RCA says the designs are far more than dreams.
"If ever you wanted an exhibition that's about the future, this is it. This is how things are going to look," said RCA rector Christopher Frayling.
Two hundred marques of car currently on the road were designed by ex-RCA students, he said, with 98 percent of alumni ending up in senior positions in industry.
SUCCESS OF FORMER STUDENTS
Former students have gone on to create successes from the luxurious Aston Martin to the innovative Ford Ka.
New Zealander Xitij Mistry sees ever-growing demand for top designers as the auto industry matures.

"You will get fashion cars that last for two or three years. They may just be a bit of plastic but they will have to look expensive and be differentiated by product designers to add extra value," Mistry said.
He has already designed a Sony car based on the core values and image of the Japanese entertainment giant, in essence creating a Sony Walkman on wheels.
"It simply couldn't be a normal car. A Sony car would have to have a twist and this has a geometric shape, like a Camcorder," said Mistry.
The hub caps resemble speakers -- they're made of the same high-perfomance rubber -- and the impression is more novelty CD-player than futuristic means of transport.

"Sony has done music, film and entertainment. It's a logical progression for them to move into another huge future market for electronics," he said. "After all, this car is really just one big gadget on wheels."
($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
